title: Health
goals: Talk about healthy and unhealthy food with a lot of, much, many, a few, a little, few and little.
Ask How much...? and How many...? about food and drinks.
Say what you have been doing lately and for how long with the present perfect continuous.
Describe feelings and things with -ed and -ing adjectives (bored / boring, tired / tiring).
Understand and use the language of a medical checkup and a prescription medicine label.
Write about your eating habits and ask for a medical appointment.

learn.title: Quantifiers: a lot of, much, many, a few, a little
learn.html:
We use quantifiers to say how much or how many of something there is. The choice depends on the noun: countable (apples, eggs, meals) or uncountable (sugar, water, rice, fruit).

MeaningCountable (plural)Uncountable
a big amounta lot of / many applesa lot of / much sugar
a small amount (enough)a few applesa little sugar
almost none (not enough)few appleslittle sugar
questionHow many apples do you eat?How much sugar do you eat?
  • a lot of is common in positive sentences. Much and many are common in negatives and questions: I don't eat much meat. Do you eat many vegetables?
  • a few / a little sound positive: I have a few minutes. few / little sound negative: I have little time. (almost none).
  • Words like water, rice, fruit, bread and advice are uncountable: use much and a little.

watch.wrong: How much apples do you eat?
watch.right: How many apples do you eat?
watch.why: Apples are countable: use How many.

watch.wrong: I drink a few water every day.
watch.right: I drink a little water every day.
watch.why: Water is uncountable: use a little, not a few.

watch.wrong: I have a little friends in this city.
watch.right: I have a few friends in this city.
watch.why: Friends is countable: use a few.

learn.title: Present perfect continuous
learn.html:
We use the present perfect continuous for an action that started in the past and is still happening now, or that has just stopped and we can see the result. It shows how long an activity has been going on.

FormExample
Positive: have / has + been + verb-ingI've been eating more vegetables.
NegativeShe hasn't been sleeping well.
QuestionHave you been exercising a lot?
How long...?How long have you been taking this medicine?
  • With for we say the length of time: for two weeks, for a long time. With since we say the starting point: since Monday, since January.
  • It is also used with lately and recently: I've been feeling tired lately.
  • State verbs (know, like, have = own) do not usually use the continuous form: I have known him for years.

watch.wrong: I am drinking more water since last week.
watch.right: I have been drinking more water since last week.
watch.why: With since / for, use the present perfect continuous, not the present continuous.

watch.wrong: She has been exercise every morning.
watch.right: She has been exercising every morning.

watch.wrong: How long do you take this medicine?
watch.right: How long have you been taking this medicine?
watch.why: To ask about the length of an action that continues until now, use have you been + -ing.

watch.wrong: He has been knowing the doctor for years.
watch.right: He has known the doctor for years.
watch.why: Know is a state verb: use the simple present perfect.

learn.title: Adjectives ending in -ed and -ing
learn.html:
Many adjectives come from verbs: bore, tire, interest, surprise, worry. They have two forms with different meanings.

EndingUseExample
-ed (bored, tired, interested)how a person feelsI'm bored. She was surprised.
-ing (boring, tiring, interesting)the thing, person or situation that causes the feelingThe movie is boring. The news was surprising.
  • Compare: The doctor was worried (she felt worry) and The results were worrying (they caused worry).
  • After be / feel / seem, use -ed for feelings: I feel relaxed.
  • Common pairs: bored / boring, tired / tiring, interested / interesting, excited / exciting, shocked / shocking, relaxed / relaxing, stressed / stressful.

watch.wrong: I am very boring in this class.
watch.right: I am very bored in this class.
watch.why: I feel bored. Boring describes the class, not my feeling.
The checkup causes the feeling, so use -ing.
A person who feels interest is interested.
The documentary causes the shock: shocking.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• I've been trying to cut down on sugar. — talking about a recent change in your habits.
  • How often do you eat fast food? / How much water do you drink? — asking about someone's habits.
  • I don't have much time to cook, so I usually eat out. — explaining a problem with healthy eating.
  • I'd like to make an appointment for a checkup. — calling a clinic.
  • I've been feeling tired lately. / I haven't been sleeping well. — telling the doctor your symptoms.
  • Do you have any allergies? / Are you taking any medicine? — typical questions at a checkup.
  • Take one tablet twice a day, with food. — instructions on a prescription label.
  • How long have you been feeling this way? — a doctor's question about symptoms.

I try to eat well, but it is not always easy. For breakfast I usually have a bowl of oatmeal with a little honey and a few strawberries. At lunch I eat a lot of vegetables, some rice and chicken or beans. I don't eat much red meat because my doctor told me to eat less of it.

My biggest problem is sugar. I have been drinking too much soda, so I've been trying to cut down since January. Now I drink a lot of water and only one soda a week. I also like snacks. In the afternoon I often eat a few nuts or an apple, but sometimes I eat cookies when I'm bored at work.

reading.title: The Sugar in Your Day
reading.intro: Read the article about sugar and answer.
paragraphs: Many people think they don't eat much sugar. They don't put a lot of it in their coffee, and they rarely eat candy. However, sugar is hiding in many foods that we do not expect. Bread, pasta sauce, yogurt, cereal and even some soups often contain added sugar. That is why many doctors say that the problem is not only the sweets we see, but also the sugar we cannot see.

Health organizations suggest that adults eat no more than about 50 grams of added sugar a day, which is around twelve teaspoons. Less is even better. A small can of soda has about 35 grams, so one drink can use most of your daily limit. Fruit juice can be a surprise too. Even when the label says "natural", a glass may have almost as much sugar as a soda.

Why is too much sugar a problem? First, sugary food gives you quick energy, but you often feel tired again an hour later. Second, it has a lot of calories and very little fiber or protein, so you feel hungry soon, and you may eat more. Over many years, a diet with too much sugar can lead to weight gain, tooth problems and diabetes.

Marta, a nurse from Guadalajara, has been trying to eat less sugar for six months. "At first it was difficult," she says. "I was always tired and bored in the afternoon, and I wanted a snack." She started reading food labels, and she was surprised by the results. Now she drinks water instead of soda, and she eats fruit or a few nuts as a snack. "I have been sleeping better, and I have more energy," she says.

You do not need to stop eating sugar completely. A good first step is to read labels and to choose foods with little added sugar. Then you can cut down slowly: use a little less sugar in your coffee, eat smaller portions of dessert, and keep sweets for special days. Small changes, made every day, are easier to keep than a strict diet.
